# Algorithm Families & Characteristics

Covers the mathematical foundations, parameter sizes, and performance of NIST PQC
algorithms. See [citations.md](../citations.md) for full source details.

## ML-KEM (FIPS 203) — Lattice-Based Key Encapsulation

Based on the Module Learning With Errors (Module-LWE) problem [4]. IND-CCA2
secure [4].

| Parameter Set | Security Level | Public Key | Ciphertext | Secret Key | Shared Secret |
|---------------|---------------|------------|------------|------------|---------------|
| ML-KEM-512 | NIST Level 1 (~AES-128) | 800 bytes | 768 bytes | 1,632 bytes | 32 bytes |
| ML-KEM-768 | NIST Level 3 (~AES-192) | 1,184 bytes | 1,088 bytes | 2,400 bytes | 32 bytes |
| ML-KEM-1024 | NIST Level 5 (~AES-256) | 1,568 bytes | 1,568 bytes | 3,168 bytes | 32 bytes |

Source: CRYSTALS-Kyber official site [4]. ML-KEM-768 is the recommended parameter
set, achieving "more than 128 bits of security against all known classical and
quantum attacks" [4].

**Performance** (Intel Core i7-4770K Haswell, AVX2) [4]:

| Operation | ML-KEM-768 Cycles |
|-----------|-------------------|
| Key generation | 52,732 |
| Encapsulation | 67,624 |
| Decapsulation | 53,156 |

## ML-DSA (FIPS 204) — Lattice-Based Digital Signatures

Based on Module-LWE and Module Short Integer Solution (Module-SIS) problems [34].

| Parameter Set | Security | Public Key | Signature | Private Key |
|---------------|----------|------------|-----------|-------------|
| ML-DSA-44 | NIST Category 2 | 1,312 bytes | 2,420 bytes | 2,560 bytes |
| ML-DSA-65 | NIST Category 3 | 1,952 bytes | 3,293 bytes | 4,032 bytes |
| ML-DSA-87 | NIST Category 5 | 2,592 bytes | 4,627 bytes | 4,896 bytes |

Source: Discovery agent cross-referencing FIPS 204 [34] and IBM documentation.

## SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) — Hash-Based Digital Signatures

Based solely on the security of cryptographic hash functions (second preimage
resistance) [8]. Stateless design. 12 parameter sets across 3 security levels,
with SHA2/SHAKE hash options and "s" (smaller signatures) / "f" (faster) variants [8].

| Security Level | Public Key | Private Key | Signature Range |
|---------------|------------|-------------|-----------------|
| Level 1 (AES-128 equiv.) | 32 bytes | 64 bytes | 7,856–17,088 bytes [8] |
| Level 3 (AES-192 equiv.) | 48 bytes | 96 bytes | 16,224–35,664 bytes [8] |
| Level 5 (AES-256 equiv.) | 64 bytes | 128 bytes | 29,792–49,856 bytes [8] |

SLH-DSA is the "most conservative choice for digital signing algorithms" [8].
Ideal for code signing; not suited for general TLS replacement due to large
signatures [8]. Standardized in FIPS 205 (August 2024) [1].

## FN-DSA (Draft FIPS 206) — NTRU Lattice-Based Signatures

Based on the Short Integer Solution (SIS) problem over NTRU lattices [5].
Uses the Gentry-Peikert-Vaikuntanathan framework [5]. EUF-CMA secure [6].

| Parameter Set | Security Level | Public Key | Signature (padded) | Secret Key |
|---------------|---------------|------------|-------------------|------------|
| Falcon-512 / FN-DSA-512 | NIST Level 1 | 897 bytes | 666 bytes | 1,281 bytes |
| Falcon-1024 / FN-DSA-1024 | NIST Level 5 | 1,793 bytes | 1,280 bytes | 2,305 bytes |

Sources: falcon-sign.info [5], OQS [6]. Note: unpadded signatures are larger
(752 / 1,462 bytes) [6].

**Performance** (Intel Core i5-8259U) [5]:

| Metric | Falcon-512 | Falcon-1024 |
|--------|-----------|-----------|
| Key generation | 8.64 ms | 27.45 ms |
| Signing throughput | 5,948 sig/s | 2,913 sig/s |
| Verification throughput | 27,933 ver/s | 13,650 ver/s |
| Key gen RAM | 14,336 bytes | 28,672 bytes |

Falcon-512 is "roughly equivalent, in classical security terms, to RSA-2048"
while achieving faster signature generation than OpenSSL's RSA [5].

## HQC — Code-Based Key Encapsulation

Based on syndrome decoding of quasi-cyclic codes (Hamming Quasi-Cyclic) [7].
IND-CCA2 secure [7].

| Parameter Set | Security Level | Public Key | Ciphertext | Secret Key | Shared Secret |
|---------------|---------------|------------|------------|------------|---------------|
| HQC-128 | NIST Level 1 | 2,249 bytes | 4,433 bytes | 2,305 bytes | 64 bytes |
| HQC-192 | NIST Level 3 | 4,522 bytes | 8,978 bytes | 4,586 bytes | 64 bytes |
| HQC-256 | NIST Level 5 | 7,245 bytes | 14,421 bytes | 7,317 bytes | 64 bytes |

Source: OQS [7]. HQC keys and ciphertexts are substantially larger than ML-KEM
but use fundamentally different mathematics, providing algorithm diversity [3].

## Size Comparison — PQC vs. Classical

| Algorithm | Public Key | Signature/Ciphertext | Use Case |
|-----------|-----------|---------------------|----------|
| RSA-2048 | 256 bytes | 256 bytes (sig) | Classical signature |
| Ed25519 | 32 bytes | 64 bytes (sig) | Classical signature |
| ECDH P-256 | 64 bytes | 64 bytes (shared) | Classical key exchange |
| ML-KEM-768 | 1,184 bytes | 1,088 bytes (ct) | PQ key encapsulation [4] |
| ML-DSA-65 | 1,952 bytes | 3,293 bytes (sig) | PQ digital signature |
| FN-DSA-512 | 897 bytes | 666 bytes (sig) | PQ digital signature [5] |
| SLH-DSA-128s | 32 bytes | 7,856 bytes (sig) | PQ digital signature [8] |
| HQC-128 | 2,249 bytes | 4,433 bytes (ct) | PQ key encapsulation [7] |

## Security Assumptions by Family

| Family | Hard Problem | Quantum Resistance Basis |
|--------|-------------|------------------------|
| Lattice (ML-KEM, ML-DSA) | Module-LWE, Module-SIS | No known efficient quantum algorithms for lattice problems [4] |
| Lattice (FN-DSA) | SIS over NTRU lattices | NTRU resisted cryptanalysis ~25 years [5] |
| Hash-based (SLH-DSA) | Hash function preimage/collision resistance | Grover provides only quadratic speedup, mitigated by key size doubling [8] |
| Code-based (HQC) | Syndrome decoding of quasi-cyclic codes | No known efficient quantum algorithms for code-based problems [7] |

## Gaps and Limitations

- ML-DSA sizes confirmed through discovery agent cross-referencing; FIPS 204 PDF
  was not directly extractable. Values are consistent across multiple secondary sources
- FN-DSA performance benchmarks are from FALCON reference implementation, not the
  final FIPS 206 standard (which may differ)
- HQC parameter sizes from OQS may differ slightly from final NIST standard (2027)
- Performance benchmarks are implementation- and platform-specific; production
  performance varies significantly with hardware and optimization level
